finding.concern: The in-progress stamp writes unconditionally on every non-plan-only dispatch, with no check of the item's current status, so it can silently overwrite a terminal or otherwise-legitimate status.
finding.location: .claude/workflows/dispatch-phase.js:1435-1450 (stamp block), and PHASE_META_SCHEMA/TASK_META_SCHEMA at lines ~1062-1090 which never fetch `status` in the first place
finding.what_fails: If `dispatch-phase` is invoked directly via the `Workflow` tool (a documented, supported entry point per docs/workflow-schemas.md's autonomous-lane section) against a phase or task that is already `done`, `wont-fix`, `reviewed`, or `blocked` — e.g. a human re-running it by mistake, or re-checking an already-finished item — Stage 0 fetches metadata (which does not include the item's current `status`), and immediately after model resolution the stamp runs `rdm phase/task update ... --status in-progress` with no guard. `rdm-core::ops::phase::apply_phase_update` (and the task equivalent) does not enforce status transitions, so a terminal `done`/`wont-fix` record is silently reopened to `in-progress` before any real work has even begun — worse than the pre-diff behavior, where dispatch-phase wrote no status at all and a stray invocation left the record untouched.
finding.why: The task's own scoping ('What this is not') only rules out using the stamp for mutual exclusion between concurrent drivers on a *not-started* phase; it says nothing about guarding a stamp against clobbering an already-terminal item, and the 'Done when' criteria never mention a status precondition. Because PHASE_META_SCHEMA/TASK_META_SCHEMA (the only data Stage 0 fetches) omit `status` entirely, the driver has no way to condition the write on the current state even if it wanted to — the omission looks incidental rather than a deliberate design choice.
finding.recommendation: Either fetch the item's current status in Stage 0 and skip (or refuse) the stamp when it is already terminal (done/wont-fix) or otherwise not not-started/in-progress, or explicitly document/accept in the ADR-level rationale that dispatch-phase is only ever invoked on active items and a direct-Workflow misuse is out of scope — the current code does neither, it just writes blindly.

historicalVerdict.rationale:
The finding's factual claims about the code are accurate — `.claude/workflows/dispatch-phase.js:1435-1450` stamps unconditionally, and `PHASE_META_SCHEMA`/`TASK_META_SCHEMA` (lines ~1062-1090) never fetch `status` — but it does not hold up as a defect in this change.

1. It is not a deviation; it is the lane's uniform contract. Every sibling entry point already stamps in-progress with no status precondition: `.claude/skills/rdm-do/SKILL.md:55-56`, `.claude/skills/rdm-dispatch-phase/SKILL.md:64`, and the distributed templates `rdm-core/src/templates/skill-dispatch-phase-cli.md:62` and `skill-do-cli.md:46-47`. The commit's stated purpose (ac0151e) is to close the *one remaining gap* so every entry point behaves identically. Adding a status precondition only in `dispatch-phase.js` would fork the status contract by driver — precisely the failure mode the task body argues against ("putting it in autopilot closes one path and forks the contract by driver").

2. The harm scenario requires deliberate misuse, and the stamp is truthful under it. Autopilot — the only automated caller — selects phases via `rdm next`, which yields actionable items, not terminal ones. The remaining path is a human hand-invoking the `Workflow` tool with an explicit already-`done` phase argument. In that case dispatch-phase proceeds to plan, implement, commit code in the worktree, and code-review it: the item genuinely *is* being worked, so `in-progress` is an accurate label, not a corrupted one. rdm deliberately does not enforce status transitions (documented in CLAUDE.md: "Transitions are not enforced — any status can move to any other"), so status is a mutable label rather than a state-machine invariant the stamp is violating.

3. The consequence is bounded and recoverable. `apply_phase_update` clears `completed`/`commit` on a terminal→non-terminal move (`rdm-core/src/ops/phase.rs:165-172`), which is the strongest part of the finding — but the workflow lane never commits to the plan repo, so the write stays staged and is trivially reverted (`rdm discard`), and the same clobber would occur via any of the sibling skill entry points today.

4. It is explicitly out of the task's scope and does not break its acceptance criteria. The "Done when" bar — observably in-progress while worked, plan-only untouched, failed stamp degrades quietly, harnesses pass — is met; the guard (`if (!planOnly)`), the try/catch, and the non-gating ack are all present and correct at lines 1435-1450. The reviewer's own recommendation reduces to "either harden beyond scope or write down the rationale," and the code comment at lines 1422-1434 already records the entry-point rationale explicitly. That makes this a scope-expansion/documentation preference, not a correctness defect in the diff.

Residual doubt (why not higher than 72): the `completed`/`commit` clearing is real data loss under the misuse path, and a status precondition would be cheap. That is a legitimate hardening idea for the whole lane — worth a separate task covering all five stamp sites — but it is not a bug this commit introduced or is responsible for.

groundTruth.evidence: The mechanical claim holds: .claude/workflows/dispatch-phase.js stamps in-progress with no status precondition and PHASE_META_SCHEMA/TASK_META_SCHEMA never fetch status. It is not a defect: rdm deliberately does not enforce status transitions (rdm-core/src/ops/phase.rs applies any status to any status), and every sibling entry point (.claude/skills/rdm-do/SKILL.md, .claude/skills/rdm-dispatch-phase/SKILL.md, rdm-core/src/templates/skill-dispatch-phase-cli.md) already stamps unconditionally — adding the guard only here would fork the contract by driver, which is the failure mode the change exists to close.

finding.concern: The regression and 'measured floor' tables all report n=1920, which does not reconcile with the document's own stated exclusion of only 6 agents out of the 1943-agent total
finding.location: docs/token-baseline.md, 'Agent context floor' section (legacy regression, corrected regression, and floor-statistics tables) and the matching `agentContextFloor.{legacyRegression,correctedRegression,measuredFloor}.n` fields in docs/token-baseline.json
finding.what_fails: Total agent records = 1943 (summed independently from the per-agent-class table's `agents` column, and confirmed via `sum(x['agentCount'] for x in byAgentClass)` against the committed JSON = 1943). All three floor-related tables explicitly state they exclude only "6 agents with a tokens value of exactly 0 — orphaned zero-usage transcript entries, not real observations" / "the same 6 zero-usage orphaned entries" and then report n=1920. 1943 − 6 = 1937, not 1920 — a 17-agent gap the document never accounts for. Every downstream conclusion drawn from these tables (the ~38.8k reported floor, the negative-intercept regression breakdown, the 'not materially revised' claim) rests on this unexplained n.
finding.why: This document's whole value proposition is being a precise, cross-footed baseline (the per-agent-class table is cross-footed to the exact token in three independent ways). An unexplained 17-record discrepancy in the sample size backing the headline 'floor' finding is exactly the kind of silent, undocumented exclusion the doc otherwise takes pains to avoid (e.g. it explicitly enumerates and justifies every other exclusion: 6 zero-tokens, 10 no-agentId fallbacks, 11 alias-model agents, killed/failed autopilot runs).
finding.recommendation: State what the additional ~17 excluded agents are (e.g. agents lacking a per-agent `toolCalls`/tool-call count needed as the regression predictor, or an overlap with the no-agentId/alias-model buckets) and correct "excluding 6" to the real exclusion criterion and count, or correct n to 1937 if 6 really is the only exclusion.

historicalVerdict.rationale: Reproduced the number from the real on-disk data via the committed instrument (scripts/lib/token-report.mjs over ~/.claude/projects, same 40-run in-scope set). Findings: 1,943 raw agent records; exactly 17 of them carry NEITHER a `tokens` nor a `toolCalls` field (7 `cached: true` agents plus 10 `state: error` agents with no transcript — the same 10 the doc enumerates as sidecar-only fallbacks); `toolCalls` is present on exactly 1,926 agents; of those, exactly 6 have `tokens === 0` (all with `toolCalls: 0`, `state: error`, and zero tokens in every deduped class — the doc's "orphaned zero-usage transcript entries", verified to be the same set under both the zero-sidecar-tokens and zero-deduped-total definitions). 1,926 − 6 = 1,920, matching all three tables exactly. So n=1920 is correct and the 17-record "gap" is not a silent exclusion but a structural impossibility: a `tokens ≈ a + b·toolCalls` regression has no predictor for an agent with no `toolCalls`, and a "first transcript request" floor has no first request for a cached or transcript-less agent. The recommendation's fallback ("correct n to 1937 if 6 really is the only exclusion") is factually impossible — those 17 records have no tokens and no toolCalls to regress. The document also does account for both categories, just not adjacent to the tables: the known-limits list gives the sidecar-only fallback count as 10, states a cached agent contributes 0 to every class, describes the floor as measured "directly from real per-agent transcripts", and names `toolCalls` as the regression predictor. No downstream conclusion (38,838 floor, negative corrected intercept, "not materially revised") is affected. What survives is a minor prose-completeness nit — the parenthetical "(excluding 6 agents with a tokens value of exactly 0)" reads as exhaustive, so a reader cannot derive 1,920 without cross-referencing the methodology section — but that is a clarity tweak to a correct figure, not the correctness defect reported, and it directly contradicts the finding's claim that the n is unexplained and the exclusion undocumented.

groundTruth.evidence: The arithmetic gap is real (docs/token-baseline.json runSet.included.totalAgentRecords is 1943, the floor tables report n=1920, and 1943-6 is 1937), but the 17-record difference is structural: 7 cached and 10 transcript-less agents carry no toolCalls at all, and a tokens ~ a + b*toolCalls regression has no predictor for them. Not a silent exclusion.

## PLAN_TARGET

Roadmap: review-gate-intent

**body:**
```
## Problem

The plan-mode severity contract says "`blocking` means the goal, approach, or
scope is wrong". But no plan dimension ever receives a statement of what the
operator wanted. `coherence` judges internal consistency, `unit-of-work` judges
sizing, and `architectural-fit`'s one external input is the project's principles
note (`CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md`) — project-wide conventions, not per-item intent.

`distribute-workflow-lane` is the worked example. Its plan was not ambiguous — it
was coherent and precise. It said "emit these files" and did exactly that, while
the roadmap's purpose was "so other projects can use them". Every dimension
passed green. **The "never guess intent" rule fires on AMBIGUITY; nothing fires
on DIVERGENCE.** A plan can be perfectly clear about the wrong thing.

This is the failure mode the wider literature calls *intent drift*: behavior
diverging from what was wanted without breaking a test or failing a gate. The
gap is an absent input, not insufficient rigor. Sharpened by contrast: reviewing
`project-agnostic-lane` produced 8 blocking findings, because that plan made
concrete checkable claims about the repo. These dimensions are strong when a
plan asserts verifiable facts and blind when it asserts none.

## The decision

**Intent is a `## Intent` section in the roadmap body, elicited from the operator
by an interview loop in `rdm-roadmap`, and read by an `intent-alignment` plan
dimension. Phases inherit their parent roadmap's intent; they never carry their
own.**

Each half of that decision closes a question the previous plan left open, and
two of them collapse blocking findings that escalated the earlier review:

- **Body section, not first-class metadata.** A section rides the existing
  `--body` / `*_update` path for free, so the `-mcp` skill variants need no new
  tool schema to write it, and `show` output stays human-readable. Core still
  gains a parser and a splice op so consumers read one tri-state instead of
  regexing prose, and so a writer can update intent without a full-body
  read-modify-write.
- **Intent lives on the roadmap; phases inherit.** Intent answers *why the whole
  effort exists*; per-phase intent would just restate the phase body. Phase JSON
  already carries its `roadmap` slug, so inheritance is a lookup, not a design
  problem. This resolves `plan-review-intent-inheritance-scope` by deciding the
  question it says must not be deferred.
- **dispatch-phase can run the dimension.** It holds `roadmapSlug` from Stage 0,
  so it can always fetch parent intent. What lacks a persisted item is the
  LLM-authored *document* under review, not the *caller* — and the caller decides
  what gets threaded. This resolves
  `plan-review-dispatch-phase-persisted-item-contradiction`. The genuine no-item
  carve-out shrinks to `--implementation-plan` invoked with no roadmap in hand.

## What the artifact is

\`\`\`markdown
## Intent

**Goal.** <the outcome the operator wants, as an observable end state — not the
mechanism that produces it>

**Non-goals.**
- <explicitly out of scope>

**Done looks like.**
- <operator-testable signal: WHEN <situation> THEN <observable outcome>>

**Interview.** (captured YYYY-MM-DD)
- Q: <question asked> → A: <operator's answer, verbatim>
\`\`\`

Three properties do the work:

- **Goal states an end state, not a mechanism.** "So other projects can use
  them" is an end state; "emit these files" is a mechanism. Divergence is only
  detectable when the two are recorded separately.
- **\`Done looks like\` is operator-testable.** Borrowed from EARS-style
  acceptance criteria: a \`WHEN/THEN\` observable a later reader can check without
  re-deriving the design.
- **The interview log is verbatim.** The gate compares a plan against the
  operator's own words, not the authoring agent's paraphrase of them — a
  paraphrase already carries the agent's reading of the goal, which is exactly
  what needs auditing.

Intent is tri-state, and the distinction is load-bearing:

| State | Written form | Gate behavior |
|---|---|---|
| absent | no \`## Intent\` section | \`blocking\` on roadmap-scoped targets |
| not captured | section body is exactly \`(not captured)\` | \`suggestion\` — explicit, greppable opt-out |
| captured | goal + non-goals + done-looks-like | alignment check runs |

\`(not captured)\` is a deliberate escape hatch with two users: a legacy roadmap
that predates the artifact, and a headless authoring path where no operator is
present to interview. It is an acknowledged gap rather than a silent one, and
\`rdm intent list\` surfaces every roadmap sitting on it — so the opt-out is
auditable instead of invisible.

## How it is captured

An interview loop in \`rdm-roadmap\`, run before phases are designed, shaped by
what works in comparable tools:

- **Bounded budget** — at most 3–5 questions, one per turn. Spec-kit's \`/clarify\`
  caps at 5; preference-elicitation work converges on one targeted question per
  turn to avoid overwhelming the respondent.
- **Prioritized by impact × uncertainty** — ask only where the answer would
  change the phase decomposition. Everything else is the agent's job to decide.
- **Closed-form questions** — 2–4 mutually exclusive options with a recommended
  default, or a short-answer with a suggested value, so the operator answers in
  one token. In Claude Code this is \`AskUserQuestion\`; the skill's
  \`allowed-tools\` must be extended to permit it.
- **Early termination** — stop on an operator signal ("done", "that's it"), or
  as soon as goal, non-goals, and a success signal are all unambiguous.
- **Never fabricate** — an unresolved high-impact question is recorded under
  \`Open\`, not guessed. If no operator answers at all, write \`(not captured)\`.

The same capture is offered from interactive \`rdm-plan-review\`, so an existing
roadmap can gain intent without being recreated.

## How the gate reads it

A new always-on plan dimension, \`intent-alignment\`, asking two questions the
existing dimensions cannot:

1. **Divergence** — could every acceptance criterion pass while \`Done looks like\`
   remains false? This is the \`distribute-workflow-lane\` check.
2. **Scope creep** — does any step pursue something the operator listed as a
   non-goal?

Missing-intent policy by caller, chosen so the gate never deadlocks a lane that
cannot supply the input:

- roadmap-scoped target (roadmap or phase), no intent on the roadmap →
  \`blocking\`; the operator fixes it by recording intent
- task with no intent → \`suggestion\` (tasks have no parent to inherit from)
- \`(not captured)\` → \`suggestion\` naming the acknowledged gap
- no roadmap in hand at all (\`--implementation-plan\`) → the alignment check does
  not run; its absence is reported as a \`suggestion\`-severity finding through the
  existing ranked-survivors array, so \`hasBlocking\` stays false and no revision
  budget is burned

Backfill (phase 3) lands **before** the gate (phase 4) precisely so turning on a
blocking rule does not paint the whole live backlog red.

## The other blind spots

Intent blindness is the largest gap but not the only one, and the rest share its
shape — each is a way a plan passes while the stated goal goes unmet:

- **Refuter laundering.** A finding can be refuted on the grounds that the defect
  is "accepted scope" or "deferred to a follow-up". A recorded deferral is
  evidence the defect is REAL, not evidence it is refuted.
- **Deferred acceptance criteria score as green.** A criterion marked deferred
  reads as met, so a plan is judged complete while the work that would achieve
  the goal is explicitly not being done.

Phase 5 carries these. They are grouped because each is a small edit to the same
canonical review source and both share one harness.

A third candidate — a generic \`portability\` dimension asking whether a change
works outside the repo it was written in — was **cut on review**. Most projects
have no reason to care, so it would couple the review mechanism to a concern
specific to this one, and it is not the problem this roadmap exists to solve.
The two defects above are properties of the review mechanism itself and hold
anywhere.

## Constraints

- **The review mechanism encodes no fact about this repo.** Dimension, refuter,
  and gate prose ships to other repos; it may describe the artifact and the
  check, never a path, crate, or project-specific trigger. Repo-specific
  build mechanics belong in phase steps, not in the mechanism.
- **Never fail closed in a lane that cannot supply the input.** A blocking
  finding on a document nobody can revise burns \`maxPlanRevise\`
  (\`lib/dispatch-phase.mjs\`, \`runPlanGate\`) and escalates every phase.
- **The shipped templates are the deliverable; the dogfood copies are not.**
  Each skill exists as a \`-cli\`/\`-mcp\` template pair under
  \`rdm-core/src/templates/\`, \`include_str!\`-embedded in \`agent_config.rs\` and
  emitted by \`rdm agent-config claude --skills\`. That pair is what an acceptance
  criterion may assert on. The \`.claude/skills/\` copies are this repo's own
  working tools and are **deliberately free to diverge** — they carry dev-build
  paths, a dev-repo banner, and locally-tuned prose, and they must stay editable
  without a downstream release. No plan in this roadmap may add a sync or
  byte-identity gate between the two, and no acceptance criterion may require a
  dogfood copy to match its template. \`verify-agent-config-distribution.sh\`
  already declares that diff out of scope and gates skills structurally
  (existence, frontmatter, cross-file reference resolution) instead; keep it
  that way.
- **Editing \`lib/review.mjs\` propagates past the generators.**
  \`gen-workflow-review.sh\` restamps the workflow consumers and
  \`gen-skill-review.sh\` rewrites the skill templates, but neither syncs the
  byte-identical twins under \`rdm-core/src/templates/workflows/\`. Those twins
  are a genuine duplicated-file contract — the same script on disk twice, one
  copy compiled into the binary — and are gated by
  \`verify-agent-config-distribution.sh\` and \`verify-workflow-review-outcome.sh\`.
  That \`cp\` is done by hand in the same commit (precedent: 75e70af). This
  applies to workflow scripts only, never to skills.

## Prior art consulted

- **GitHub spec-kit \`/clarify\`** — 5-question cap, a 9-category ambiguity
  taxonomy scored Clear/Partial/Missing, multiple-choice questions with a
  recommended option, answers recorded verbatim into a \`## Clarifications\`
  section and then propagated into the spec proper.
- **AWS Kiro specs** — \`requirements.md\` generated up front as user stories with
  EARS (\`WHEN … THE SYSTEM SHALL …\`) acceptance criteria, "precise enough for an
  agent to implement without guessing your intent".
- **Preference-elicitation research** (TO-GATE; Google's clarifying-questions
  work) — jointly optimize *which* question to ask against task completion; one
  targeted question per turn; terminate when the specification is unambiguous.
- **Intent- and goal-drift literature** — divergence from specification that
  breaks no test and fails no pipeline; detectable only by comparing behavior
  against a recorded statement of what was wanted.

## Relation to other work

- Split out of \`project-agnostic-lane\` phase 5, which plan review ESCALATED on
  five blocking findings. That phase is \`wont-fix\` pointing here.
- Resolves \`plan-review-intent-inheritance-scope\` and
  \`plan-review-dispatch-phase-persisted-item-contradiction\` by decision rather
  than by implementation; both are closed against this rewrite.
- \`classify-outcome-ac-table-channel\` (closing the gap between
  \`classifyOutcome\`'s spec prose and its blocking-only input) stays a separate
  task and is explicitly out of scope in phase 5.
- Depends on nothing in \`project-agnostic-lane\`; the two can proceed in parallel.
  Where this roadmap adds review-dimension prose, it must land AFTER that
  roadmap's phase 1 makes dimension prose language-neutral, or repeat the same
  genericity discipline.

**body:**

## Problem

The plan-mode severity contract says "`blocking` means the goal, approach, or
scope is wrong". But no plan dimension ever receives a statement of what the
operator wanted. `coherence` judges internal consistency, `unit-of-work` judges
sizing, and `architectural-fit`'s one external input is the project's principles
note (`CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md`) — project-wide conventions, not per-item intent.

`distribute-workflow-lane` is the worked example. Its plan was not ambiguous — it
was coherent and precise. It said "emit these files" and did exactly that, while
the roadmap's purpose was "so other projects can use them". Every dimension
passed green. **The "never guess intent" rule fires on AMBIGUITY; nothing fires
on DIVERGENCE.** A plan can be perfectly clear about the wrong thing.

This is the failure mode the wider literature calls *intent drift*: behavior
diverging from what was wanted without breaking a test or failing a gate. The
gap is an absent input, not insufficient rigor. Sharpened by contrast: reviewing
`project-agnostic-lane` produced 8 blocking findings, because that plan made
concrete checkable claims about the repo. These dimensions are strong when a
plan asserts verifiable facts and blind when it asserts none.

## The decision

**Intent is a `## Intent` section in the roadmap body, elicited from the operator
by an interview loop in `rdm-roadmap`, and read by an `intent-alignment` plan
dimension. Phases inherit their parent roadmap's intent; they never carry their
own.**

Each half of that decision closes a question the previous plan left open, and
two of them collapse blocking findings that escalated the earlier review:

- **Body section, not first-class metadata.** A section rides the existing
  `--body` / `*_update` path for free, so the `-mcp` skill variants need no new
  tool schema to write it, and `show` output stays human-readable. Core still
  gains a parser and a splice op so consumers read one tri-state instead of
  regexing prose, and so a writer can update intent without a full-body
  read-modify-write.
- **Intent lives on the roadmap; phases inherit.** Intent answers *why the whole
  effort exists*; per-phase intent would just restate the phase body. Phase JSON
  already carries its `roadmap` slug, so inheritance is a lookup, not a design
  problem. This resolves `plan-review-intent-inheritance-scope` by deciding the
  question it says must not be deferred.
- **dispatch-phase can run the dimension.** It holds `roadmapSlug` from Stage 0,
  so it can always fetch parent intent. What lacks a persisted item is the
  LLM-authored *document* under review, not the *caller* — and the caller decides
  what gets threaded. This resolves
  `plan-review-dispatch-phase-persisted-item-contradiction`. The genuine no-item
  carve-out shrinks to `--implementation-plan` invoked with no roadmap in hand.

## What the artifact is

\`\`\`markdown
## Intent

**Goal.** <the outcome the operator wants, as an observable end state — not the
mechanism that produces it>

**Non-goals.**
- <explicitly out of scope>

**Done looks like.**
- <operator-testable signal: WHEN <situation> THEN <observable outcome>>

**Interview.** (captured YYYY-MM-DD)
- Q: <question asked> → A: <operator's answer, verbatim>
\`\`\`

Three properties do the work:

- **Goal states an end state, not a mechanism.** "So other projects can use
  them" is an end state; "emit these files" is a mechanism. Divergence is only
  detectable when the two are recorded separately.
- **\`Done looks like\` is operator-testable.** Borrowed from EARS-style
  acceptance criteria: a \`WHEN/THEN\` observable a later reader can check without
  re-deriving the design.
- **The interview log is verbatim.** The gate compares a plan against the
  operator's own words, not the authoring agent's paraphrase of them — a
  paraphrase already carries the agent's reading of the goal, which is exactly
  what needs auditing.

Intent is tri-state, and the distinction is load-bearing:

| State | Written form | Gate behavior |
|---|---|---|
| absent | no \`## Intent\` section | \`blocking\` on roadmap-scoped targets |
| not captured | section body is exactly \`(not captured)\` | \`suggestion\` — explicit, greppable opt-out |
| captured | goal + non-goals + done-looks-like | alignment check runs |

\`(not captured)\` is a deliberate escape hatch with two users: a legacy roadmap
that predates the artifact, and a headless authoring path where no operator is
present to interview. It is an acknowledged gap rather than a silent one, and
\`rdm intent list\` surfaces every roadmap sitting on it — so the opt-out is
auditable instead of invisible.

## How it is captured

An interview loop in \`rdm-roadmap\`, run before phases are designed, shaped by
what works in comparable tools:

- **Bounded budget** — at most 3–5 questions, one per turn. Spec-kit's \`/clarify\`
  caps at 5; preference-elicitation work converges on one targeted question per
  turn to avoid overwhelming the respondent.
- **Prioritized by impact × uncertainty** — ask only where the answer would
  change the phase decomposition. Everything else is the agent's job to decide.
- **Closed-form questions** — 2–4 mutually exclusive options with a recommended
  default, or a short-answer with a suggested value, so the operator answers in
  one token. In Claude Code this is \`AskUserQuestion\`; the skill's
  \`allowed-tools\` must be extended to permit it.
- **Early termination** — stop on an operator signal ("done", "that's it"), or
  as soon as goal, non-goals, and a success signal are all unambiguous.
- **Never fabricate** — an unresolved high-impact question is recorded under
  \`Open\`, not guessed. If no operator answers at all, write \`(not captured)\`.

The same capture is offered from interactive \`rdm-plan-review\`, so an existing
roadmap can gain intent without being recreated.

## How the gate reads it

A new always-on plan dimension, \`intent-alignment\`, asking two questions the
existing dimensions cannot:

1. **Divergence** — could every acceptance criterion pass while \`Done looks like\`
   remains false? This is the \`distribute-workflow-lane\` check.
2. **Scope creep** — does any step pursue something the operator listed as a
   non-goal?

Missing-intent policy by caller, chosen so the gate never deadlocks a lane that
cannot supply the input:

- roadmap-scoped target (roadmap or phase), no intent on the roadmap →
  \`blocking\`; the operator fixes it by recording intent
- task with no intent → \`suggestion\` (tasks have no parent to inherit from)
- \`(not captured)\` → \`suggestion\` naming the acknowledged gap
- no roadmap in hand at all (\`--implementation-plan\`) → the alignment check does
  not run; its absence is reported as a \`suggestion\`-severity finding through the
  existing ranked-survivors array, so \`hasBlocking\` stays false and no revision
  budget is burned

Backfill (phase 3) lands **before** the gate (phase 4) precisely so turning on a
blocking rule does not paint the whole live backlog red.

## The other blind spots

Intent blindness is the largest gap but not the only one, and the rest share its
shape — each is a way a plan passes while the stated goal goes unmet:

- **Refuter laundering.** A finding can be refuted on the grounds that the defect
  is "accepted scope" or "deferred to a follow-up". A recorded deferral is
  evidence the defect is REAL, not evidence it is refuted.
- **Deferred acceptance criteria score as green.** A criterion marked deferred
  reads as met, so a plan is judged complete while the work that would achieve
  the goal is explicitly not being done.

Phase 5 carries these. They are grouped because each is a small edit to the same
canonical review source and both share one harness.

A third candidate — a generic \`portability\` dimension asking whether a change
works outside the repo it was written in — was **cut on review**. Most projects
have no reason to care, so it would couple the review mechanism to a concern
specific to this one, and it is not the problem this roadmap exists to solve.
The two defects above are properties of the review mechanism itself and hold
anywhere.

## Constraints

- **The review mechanism encodes no fact about this repo.** Dimension, refuter,
  and gate prose ships to other repos; it may describe the artifact and the
  check, never a path, crate, or project-specific trigger. Repo-specific
  build mechanics belong in phase steps, not in the mechanism.
- **Never fail closed in a lane that cannot supply the input.** A blocking
  finding on a document nobody can revise burns \`maxPlanRevise\`
  (\`lib/dispatch-phase.mjs\`, \`runPlanGate\`) and escalates every phase.
- **The shipped templates are the deliverable; the dogfood copies are not.**
  Each skill exists as a \`-cli\`/\`-mcp\` template pair under
  \`rdm-core/src/templates/\`, \`include_str!\`-embedded in \`agent_config.rs\` and
  emitted by \`rdm agent-config claude --skills\`. That pair is what an acceptance
  criterion may assert on. The \`.claude/skills/\` copies are this repo's own
  working tools and are **deliberately free to diverge** — they carry dev-build
  paths, a dev-repo banner, and locally-tuned prose, and they must stay editable
  without a downstream release. No plan in this roadmap may add a sync or
  byte-identity gate between the two, and no acceptance criterion may require a
  dogfood copy to match its template. \`verify-agent-config-distribution.sh\`
  already declares that diff out of scope and gates skills structurally
  (existence, frontmatter, cross-file reference resolution) instead; keep it
  that way.
- **Editing \`lib/review.mjs\` propagates past the generators.**
  \`gen-workflow-review.sh\` restamps the workflow consumers and
  \`gen-skill-review.sh\` rewrites the skill templates, but neither syncs the
  byte-identical twins under \`rdm-core/src/templates/workflows/\`. Those twins
  are a genuine duplicated-file contract — the same script on disk twice, one
  copy compiled into the binary — and are gated by
  \`verify-agent-config-distribution.sh\` and \`verify-workflow-review-outcome.sh\`.
  That \`cp\` is done by hand in the same commit (precedent: 75e70af). This
  applies to workflow scripts only, never to skills.

## Prior art consulted

- **GitHub spec-kit \`/clarify\`** — 5-question cap, a 9-category ambiguity
  taxonomy scored Clear/Partial/Missing, multiple-choice questions with a
  recommended option, answers recorded verbatim into a \`## Clarifications\`
  section and then propagated into the spec proper.
- **AWS Kiro specs** — \`requirements.md\` generated up front as user stories with
  EARS (\`WHEN … THE SYSTEM SHALL …\`) acceptance criteria, "precise enough for an
  agent to implement without guessing your intent".
- **Preference-elicitation research** (TO-GATE; Google's clarifying-questions
  work) — jointly optimize *which* question to ask against task completion; one
  targeted question per turn; terminate when the specification is unambiguous.
- **Intent- and goal-drift literature** — divergence from specification that
  breaks no test and fails no pipeline; detectable only by comparing behavior
  against a recorded statement of what was wanted.

## Relation to other work

- Split out of \`project-agnostic-lane\` phase 5, which plan review ESCALATED on
  five blocking findings. That phase is \`wont-fix\` pointing here.
- Resolves \`plan-review-intent-inheritance-scope\` and
  \`plan-review-dispatch-phase-persisted-item-contradiction\` by decision rather
  than by implementation; both are closed against this rewrite.
- \`classify-outcome-ac-table-channel\` (closing the gap between
  \`classifyOutcome\`'s spec prose and its blocking-only input) stays a separate
  task and is explicitly out of scope in phase 5.
- Depends on nothing in \`project-agnostic-lane\`; the two can proceed in parallel.
  Where this roadmap adds review-dimension prose, it must land AFTER that
  roadmap's phase 1 makes dimension prose language-neutral, or repeat the same
  genericity discipline.
```

## Context

~8 dimension blocks in `.claude/workflows/lib/review.mjs` hardcode rdm's own Rust
conventions into what is supposed to be a generic reviewer: `correctness` cites
rdm-core/anyhow error policy; `architecture` cites "logic in rdm-core with
cli/server as thin layers"; `api-docs` cites `#![warn(missing_docs)]` and rustdoc
`# Errors`/`# Panics`/`# Safety`; `changelog` asserts a CHANGELOG.md entry is
mandatory per CLAUDE.md.

SILENT breakage: a JS consumer repo gets a reviewer applying rustdoc rules. It
reaches two surfaces — `gen-workflow-review.sh` stamps the JS into three workflow
consumers, and `gen-skill-review.sh` renders the `//|` prose into
`skill-review-{cli,mcp}.md`, which SHIP.

**Design revised after plan review.** The original plan extended the emit-time
substitution pass to workflow content. That is unworkable and was found blocking:
`.claude/workflows/*.js` is both the template and the executed file, so a
`{principles}` placeholder would sit literally unsubstituted in the file rdm
itself runs; and any emit-time substitution breaks the byte-identity gates that
this roadmap otherwise leaves green. Confirmed separately: `principles_file` is an
`agent-config` CLI flag only (rdm-cli/src/cli.rs:160-162) and is absent from
`Config` (rdm-core/src/config.rs), so nothing persists a principles path.

Instead, conventions reach the reviewer the way `architectural-fit` ALREADY does
it: the dimension prose instructs the AGENT to read the project's principles file,
falling back to CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md. Agents can read files; the JS does not need
to. No substitution pass, no placeholder, no gate change.

### Scope boundary (what this phase does NOT touch)

This phase rewrites **dimension prose** — each dimension's `focus` string and its
`//|` spec lines in `lib/review.mjs` — plus the config/principles plumbing in
steps 2-4. Two categories of rdm-specific text living inside the same files are
explicitly OUT of scope, and are excluded from this phase's grep criteria:

- The `rdm-core/src/` path regex in `publicApiChanged`/`deriveSignals`
  (`lib/review.mjs`, stamped into all three consumers) — owned by phase 3

  and the hand-written driver-region prose in `dispatch-phase.js` (the

## Context

Phase 3 removes the mechanical agents that can be eliminated outright. Some cannot: a call site with no caller to hoist to and no adjacent agent to absorb it is irreducible, and phase 3's classification table names that set. This phase trims what those remaining agents cost per invocation.

Given a ~36.8k-token intercept per agent before any work is done, per-agent context is the whole cost of a mechanical agent. Two Workflow-runtime options address it and **neither is used anywhere** under `.claude/workflows/`:

- `opts.agentType` — resolves against the same registry as the Agent tool, so a purpose-built agent definition can carry a trimmed system prompt and a restricted tool list. A mechanical fetch agent needs Bash and `StructuredOutput`; it does not need Edit, Write, NotebookEdit, Artifact, or Task, and every unused tool's schema is paid for on every agent.
- `opts.effort` — `'low'` is appropriate here and only here. These agents make no judgment call; they run a command and transcribe its output. This is deliberately **not** applied to finders or refuters, whose task is exactly the judgment that low effort degrades.

### This phase is feasibility-gated

Neither `agentType` nor `effort:` appears anywhere under `.claude/workflows/` today, so this is a greenfield spike against runtime capability this project has never exercised. Two questions are open and must be answered **first**, because the answers determine whether there is a change to make at all:

1. Is the `agentType` registry reachable from the Workflow runtime, and does a custom agent definition actually resolve there?
2. Is the project `CLAUDE.md` (~11.7k tokens) loaded into a custom `agentType` subagent, and how much does that move the floor?

A recorded negative result is a **legitimate completion of this phase**, on the same terms the refuter-model-tiering phase grants itself: if the registry is unreachable, or if `CLAUDE.md` loads unavoidably and the remaining trim is not worth the maintenance surface, the phase lands the measurement and the written finding and stops. It does not restructure `CLAUDE.md` speculatively, and it does not leave phase 3's completed elimination work stranded — that work has already landed independently.

### Distribution surface

The same constraint phase 3 operates under applies here. `autopilot.js`, `dispatch-phase.js` and `review-refute-fix.js` have hand-maintained byte-identical copies under `rdm-core/src/templates/workflows/` embedded by `rdm-core/src/agent_config.rs` via `include_str!`, and **no generator writes them**. Any workflow `.js` edited here must be re-synced by hand or `scripts/verify-agent-config-distribution.sh` and `scripts/verify-workflow-review-outcome.sh` hard-fail, and CI runs every `scripts/verify-*.sh`.

## Steps

1. **Feasibility check, before any implementation.** Follow whatever registry mechanism `agentType` resolves against and confirm it is reachable from the Workflow runtime. Record the answer. If it is not reachable, record that finding, skip to step 7, and complete the phase on the negative result.
2. Determine empirically whether the project `CLAUDE.md` is loaded into a custom `agentType` subagent, and by how much it moves the per-agent floor. If it is unavoidable, record that as a finding and stop pursuing it — do not restructure `CLAUDE.md` speculatively. Fold the measured floor into the step 6 decision about whether the change is worth keeping.
3. Define a mechanical subagent type with a minimal system prompt and the smallest tool set that still lets it run a command and return structured output, for the call sites phase 3 classified irreducible.
4. Thread `agentType` and `effort: 'low'` through those remaining mechanical `agent()` call sites, honouring each call site's maintenance route from phase 3's table: keep a lib the single source and re-run its generator where the site is stamped, and edit both halves of a byte-identical copied driver region where it is not.
5. Verify no judgment agent is touched: finders, refuters, planners, implementers and the plan-review `act` step keep their current model and default effort. `scripts/verify-workflow-review.sh` §5b-mechanical already asserts `act:*` must not be pinned — that assertion must still pass unchanged.
6. Re-sync `rdm-core/src/templates/workflows/{autopilot,dispatch-phase,review-refute-fix}.js` from `.claude/workflows/` for every one of those files this phase touched, and run `bash scripts/verify-agent-config-distribution.sh` and `bash scripts/verify-workflow-review-outcome.sh` to confirm byte-identity is restored.

Extend the relevant `verify-workflow-*.sh` harnesses to assert that remaining mechanical call sites carry the new options and that judgment call sites do not, with planted-mutation self-tests in both directions. If the phase completed on a negative result, this step is not applicable and the finding stands in its place.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Whether the `agentType` registry is reachable from the Workflow runtime is answered explicitly and written down, before any call site is edited.
- [ ] Whether `CLAUDE.md` loads into a custom `agentType` subagent is answered empirically and written down, with its effect on the per-agent floor quantified.
- [ ] **If step 1 establishes the registry is reachable:** every mechanical `agent()` call site that remains after phase 3 passes the mechanical `agentType` and `effort: 'low'`; no judgment call site does. **If it is not reachable**, this criterion is satisfied instead by the recorded negative result and no call site is edited.

## Context

~8 dimension blocks in `.claude/workflows/lib/review.mjs` hardcode rdm's own Rust
conventions into what is supposed to be a generic reviewer:

- `correctness` (:133) — "In rdm-core, errors must be hand-written matchable enums

- `architecture` (:150) — "Does logic live in rdm-core with cli/server as thin
  layers?"
- `api-docs` (:161) — "Public items in rdm-core must carry doc comments
  (#![warn(missing_docs)])... `# Errors`... `# Panics`... `# Safety`."
- `changelog` (:174) — asserts a CHANGELOG.md entry is mandatory per CLAUDE.md.

This is SILENT breakage: a JS consumer repo gets a reviewer confidently applying
rustdoc rules. It reaches two surfaces, not one — `gen-workflow-review.sh` stamps
the JS into three workflow consumers, and `gen-skill-review.sh` renders the `//|`
prose into `skill-review-{cli,mcp}.md`, which SHIP.

The `principles_file` mechanism (agent_config.rs:167, :218) already exists for
exactly this and is preserved. Its gap: skills get a substitution pass,
workflow content does not.

Decision (settled, do not re-litigate): ship BOTH channels with principles as the
default. Generic dimensions read `principles_file`; an optional per-dimension
config override serves projects wanting structured control.

## Steps

1. Rewrite each dimension's `focus` and `//|` prose to state generic INTENT — the
   error-handling conventions that apply, the project's layering contract, the
   documentation requirements the project states — with no language or crate names.
2. Extend the emit-time substitution pass to workflow content so `{principles}`
   and per-dimension overrides reach `.claude/workflows/*.js`, not just skills.
   Correct the false rationale at agent_config.rs:236-238 while here (the full
   doc/callout correction lands in phase 6).
3. Add the per-dimension config override surface; define precedence explicitly
   (per-dimension config > principles_file > generic default).
4. Author rdm's own principles content carrying the Rust conventions removed in
   step 1, so rdm's review loses nothing and stops being special-cased in prose.
5. Re-run `scripts/gen-workflow-review.sh` and `scripts/gen-skill-review.sh` in
   BOTH `--mode code` and `--mode plan`; confirm `verify-workflow-review.sh` green.

- [ ] A grep for `rdm-core|anyhow|rustdoc|# Panics|# Safety` over the emitted
      `skill-review-{cli,mcp}.md` and the three stamped workflow consumers returns
      zero hits
- [ ] Workflow content receives the same substitution pass as skill content;
      `{principles}` resolves in an emitted `.claude/workflows/*.js`
- [ ] Per-dimension config overrides resolve with documented precedence, covered
      by tests including the "no principles, no override" generic-default path
- [ ] rdm's own principles content carries every convention removed from the
      dimension prose; a review of an rdm diff still raises the same
      error-handling / layering / doc-section findings it did before
- [ ] `scripts/verify-workflow-review.sh` passes, including both skill projection

phase project-agnostic-lane/phase-6-downstream-execution-harness

## Context

`scripts/verify-agent-config-distribution.sh` is the gate that was supposed to
prove the lane ships correctly. It emits under `--project distro-check` —
deliberately non-rdm — and then (item 3 of its header) asserts the emitted
workflow scripts are BYTE-IDENTICAL to this repo's own copies. It held the
disproof in its hands and encoded it as the contract.

Byte-identity is the wrong invariant for a portability goal: it GUARANTEES that
rdm-specific content travels verbatim and asserts that as correct. The harness
header even names the cause out loud — "the scripts hardcode a target repo's own
binary path" — while using it to justify a different assertion.

Phase 4 relaxes those assertions as a side effect of parameterization. This phase
replaces the contract with one that could actually have caught the bug: EXECUTE
the emitted lane against a repo that is neither rdm nor Rust.

Also closes out the documentation defects: the non-sequitur at
agent_config.rs:236-238 ("no substitution pass, SINCE the Workflow runtime cannot
import/require" — unrelated; the import limit explains build-time stamping of
`lib/*.mjs`, not why an emit-time `.replace()` is impossible), and
`docs/workflow-schemas.md`'s Scope callout, which still describes the hardcoding
as accepted scope.

## Steps

1. Stand up a hermetic non-rdm, non-Rust fixture repo (temp dirs, no network) with
   its own plan repo, project name, and a small source tree in another language.
2. Emit the lane into it with the real binary and assert structural validity as
   today, but replace byte-identity with substitution-correctness: emitted ==
   template with this target's substitutions applied.
3. EXECUTE the emitted pipeline's pure logic against that fixture — drive
   `deriveSignals`, `selectDimensions`, and the command builders with the
   fixture's real file lists and diffs, asserting the conditional dimensions
   actually fire and every built command names the fixture's binary and project.
4. Add a planted-corruption self-test proving the new gate is not vacuous —
   reintroduce an rdm-specific literal and assert the harness goes red.
5. Correct the rationale at agent_config.rs:236-238 and rewrite the
   `docs/workflow-schemas.md` Scope callout to describe the shipped state.
6. Mark `workflow-lane-hardening/phase-5-parameterize-workflow-scripts-rdm-binary`
   `wont-fix` with a pointer to this roadmap; leave that roadmap's phases 1-4 alone.
7. Update CHANGELOG.md for the user-facing change: the lane now works in an
   arbitrary consumer repo.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] A hermetic non-rdm, non-Rust fixture repo is created and torn down by the
      harness; the run never touches this repo's working tree
- [ ] The byte-identity assertion is replaced by substitution-correctness against
      that fixture's project and binary
- [ ] The harness EXECUTES the emitted pipeline's pure logic and asserts the
      conditional dimensions fire on the fixture's own diffs
- [ ] Every rdm command built during that run names the fixture's binary and
      project — zero `./target/debug/rdm` or `--project rdm` occurrences
- [ ] REGRESSION TEST: reintroducing an rdm-specific literal turns the harness
      red, proving the gate is not vacuous
- [ ] agent_config.rs:236-238 no longer states the import limitation as the reason
      for absent substitution
- [ ] `docs/workflow-schemas.md`'s Scope callout describes the shipped state and
      no longer lists the hardcoding as accepted scope
- [ ] `workflow-lane-hardening` phase 5 is `wont-fix` with a pointer here; its
      phases 1-4 are untouched
- [ ] CHANGELOG.md carries a user-facing entry under [Unreleased]
- [ ] Full CI-equivalent suite passes: `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy -- -D
      warnings`, `cargo test`, and every `scripts/verify-*.sh`

Capturing the `agent()` directives from that run surfaces prompt text containing 5 `./target/debug/rdm` and 1 `--project rdm` occurrences — exactly the assertion surface AC #3/#4 require — with zero changes to templates, generators, or their --check drift gates. Additionally, even the feared export-shim route is fail-loud by ESM semantics (a missing named symbol is a static early error), making the finding's recommended non-vacuity AC largely redundant; and scratch-copy manipulation is existing precedent (verify-agent-config-distribution.sh:194-207, verify-workflow-review.sh section 1b). What survives is a minor documentation nit — the phase body does not name the bridging mechanism — not a unit-of-work boundary violation. phase workflow-lane-hardening/phase-1-prefix-workflow-engines-to-distinguish-from-skills

## Problem

The workflow-lane engines under `.claude/workflows/` (`autopilot.js`, `dispatch-phase.js`, `review-refute-fix.js`) surface with **bare names** (`autopilot`, `dispatch-phase`, `review-refute-fix`) in the skill / slash-command listing — colliding conceptually with their `rdm-*` skill front doors. A user asked "to run autopilot do I use `/autopilot` or `/rdm-autopilot`?" — the answer (`rdm-autopilot` is the front door; `autopilot` is the engine it drives via the Workflow tool) is non-obvious from the names alone.

## Fix

Give the workflow engines a distinguishing prefix so the split is unambiguous — skills are `rdm-<name>` (front door), engines are `<prefix>-<name>`. **Recommended prefix: `wf-`** (`wf-autopilot`, `wf-dispatch-phase`, `wf-review-refute-fix`); alternatives `rdm-wf-` or `engine-` — final pick is the reviewer's call.

## Scope — every reference resolves by workflow name, so all must move together

- Rename the scripts: `.claude/workflows/{autopilot,dispatch-phase,review-refute-fix}.js`.
- Update the shim invocations: `rdm-autopilot`/`rdm-dispatch-phase` SKILL.md call `Workflow({ name: "autopilot" / "dispatch-phase", ... })` — the `name` must match the new engine name.
- Update the **nested** `workflow()` call: `autopilot.js` invokes `workflow('dispatch-phase', ...)`.
- Update `scripts/gen-workflow-review.sh` consumer list (stamps into `review-refute-fix.js` + `dispatch-phase.js`) and the lib header path comments.
- Update the verify harnesses that reference the scripts by path/name: `verify-workflow-{review,dispatch,autopilot,do-auto}.sh`.
- Update docs: `CLAUDE.md` (Workflow-tool orchestration section), `docs/workflow-schemas.md`, `docs/autonomous-loop.md`.

## Note

Coordinate with the `unify-code-review` roadmap — it relocates `review-refute-fix.mjs` to `review.mjs` and touches the same generator/harness reference sites. Sequence this rename after that lands (or fold it in) to avoid double-churning the same files.

## Acceptance criteria

- Each workflow engine carries the distinguishing prefix; the `rdm-*` front-door skills are unchanged.
- Every reference (shim `Workflow({name})` calls, nested `workflow()` call, generator consumer list, verify harnesses, docs) updated in lockstep.
- `gen-workflow-review.sh --check` and all `scripts/verify-workflow-*.sh` pass.

## Context

The `security` dimension is currently gated by two Rust-only pattern lists in
`lib/review.mjs` (:571-583):

- `SECURITY_DIFF_PATTERNS` = `std::process`, `Command::new`, `std::fs::`,
  `env::var`, `from_utf8_unchecked`, `set_permissions`
- `hasUnsafe` greps `/\bunsafe\b/`

In a JS repo, `child_process.exec` never trips `securitySurface` and `hasUnsafe`
is meaningless — the dimension silently never fires. These greps are also the
wrong shape of check independent of language: they LLM-encode what a static
linter (clippy) already does, rather than asking a security question.

Claude Code's shipped security skill is the model
(`~/.claude/plugins/marketplaces/claude-plugins-official/plugins/claude-security/agents/scan-researcher.md`
— read it before starting). Its framing: "a finding is a claim that an attacker
can do something they should not be able to do, and you must be able to point at
the code that lets them — not lint, not style, not 'consider using a safer API'."

Decisive argument for dropping the greps: that skill's language-neutral `memory`
category already covers `unsafe-ffi`, `use-after-free`, and `out-of-bounds-*`
generically. The eight Rust patterns buy no coverage a generic taxonomy lacks.

## Steps

1. Read the reference agent and extract the reusable pieces: the category
   vocabulary (injection / authorization / memory / crypto / exposure), the
   impact-based HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW severity ladder, and the `(file, line, category)`
   dedupe key.
2. Rewrite the `security` dimension `focus` and `//|` prose on the threat-model
   framing — an attacker capability plus the code that grants it — with the
   category vocabulary replacing the pattern lists. Explicitly exclude lint and
   style findings.
3. Delete `SECURITY_DIFF_PATTERNS` and the `hasUnsafe` grep. Decide and document
   how `securitySurface` triggers now (phase 3 owns the general signal rework;
   this phase owns the security-specific decision).
4. Adopt "the repository is not talking to you" prompt-injection hygiene: our
   reviewers read plan documents and diffs, which are untrusted input, and must
   treat them as data under review rather than instructions.
5. Reconcile the severity ladder with the existing `blocking | concern |
   suggestion` contract — map, do not duplicate.
6. Re-run both generators; confirm the harness is green.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `SECURITY_DIFF_PATTERNS` and the `\bunsafe\b` grep are gone from
      `lib/review.mjs` and every stamped consumer
- [ ] The security dimension prose contains no language-specific API or token
      names and states the attacker-capability framing explicitly
- [ ] The category vocabulary is enumerated in the dimension, and findings carry a
      category slug usable as part of a `(file, line, category)` dedupe key
- [ ] Severity maps onto the existing `blocking | concern | suggestion` contract
      with the mapping documented, not a second parallel ladder
- [ ] The dimension carries explicit prompt-injection hygiene: repository and plan
      content is data under review, never instructions
- [ ] A seeded non-Rust diff containing a real command-injection sink triggers the
      security dimension and produces a finding; a seeded pure-style diff does not
- [ ] `scripts/verify-workflow-review.sh` passes

finding.concern: When `estimate.js` (or any consumer of `buildEstimatePipeline`) is invoked with a `phase` narrowing argument, every phase that wasn't targeted this run — including phases that are genuinely still unestimated — is unconditionally reported as 'skipped, already estimated'.
finding.location: .claude/workflows/lib/estimate.mjs:226-232 (buildEstimatePipeline) and :277-294 (buildEstimateSummaryText), byte-copied into .claude/workflows/estimate.js and .claude/workflows/lib/autopilot.mjs
finding.what_fails: Given a roadmap with phase 1 and phase 2 both unestimated, running `estimate.js` with `{ roadmap, phase: 1 }` produces `summary.skipped = ['phase-2-b', ...]` and `buildEstimateSummaryText` renders it under the heading 'skipped, already estimated (N): phase-2-b, ...' — even though phase-2-b has NEVER been estimated. Reproduced directly: `buildEstimatePipeline` computes `skipped = allStems.filter(s => !ratedSet.has(s))` where `ratedSet` is built from `targetStems` (the phases selected AND narrowed this run), not from which phases actually already carry a difficulty. Any phase excluded purely by the `phase` narrow — not because it was already estimated — lands in the same bucket and gets the same misleading label.
finding.why: The pipeline conflates two semantically different populations into one `skipped` array: (a) phases that are genuinely already estimated (should stay unrated forever, this label is correct), and (b) phases that are merely out of scope for this particular narrowed run (still need estimating on a future pass). `buildEstimateSummaryText` then hard-codes the human-readable label as 'already estimated' for the whole array, so a human or an automation reading the workflow's printed/returned summary after a `--phase`-narrowed run is told phases were 'already estimated' when they were not — this can lead a user to believe a roadmap is fully estimated when it isn't, or an autopilot-adjacent surface reading this summary to skip a phase that in fact still needs rating.
finding.recommendation: Distinguish the two cases in the returned summary, e.g. split into `skipped` (already had difficulty/model set) and a separate `notTargeted`/`deferred` bucket (excluded only by the `phase` narrow), and update `buildEstimateSummaryText` to label each accurately. The existing harness test at scripts/verify-workflow-estimate.sh ~line 353 ('narrow to a single phase number') only asserts array membership, not the summary text's truthfulness, so it did not catch this — add an assertion on the rendered summary text (or the new field) for a narrowed run with other unestimated phases present.

historicalVerdict.rationale: Verified against the actual implementation at .claude/workflows/lib/estimate.mjs (roadmap/headless-skill-workflows worktree, commit 620dcb2). # Phase 4: Parameterize the rdm binary and project as runtime arguments (monorepo-safe)

## Context

Absorbs `workflow-lane-hardening/phase-5-parameterize-workflow-scripts-rdm-binary`,
which covers only the mechanical half of this.

Every rdm invocation in the three shipped scripts hardcodes `./target/debug/rdm`,
and every *project-scoped* one hardcodes `--project rdm`. The raw counts differ
per file (dispatch-phase.js: 17 binary sites vs 7 `--project rdm` sites;
autopilot.js: 13 vs 12), but that delta is NOT a defect — it is exactly the
`rdm model resolve` calls, which is a project-agnostic subcommand that does not
accept `--project` at all (`./target/debug/rdm model resolve plan --project rdm`
errors with `unexpected argument '--project' found`). `rdm commit`/`status`/
`discard` are in the same class — CLAUDE.md already documents them as operating
on the whole plan repo's git state and taking no `--project`. So the current
state IS internally consistent, and this phase is purely a parameterization, not
a bug fix.

**Design revised after plan review.** The original emit-time `{rdm_bin}`
placeholder was unworkable: `.claude/workflows/*.js` is simultaneously the
template `generate_workflows()` `include_str!`s and the file the Workflow tool
executes, with no emit step in rdm's own loop — a placeholder would sit literally
unsubstituted in the file rdm itself runs. Both axes are therefore RUNTIME
arguments. See the roadmap body's Approach section.

Runtime args change no bytes, so the byte-identity gates
(`generate_workflows_are_byte_identical_to_source`, agent_config.rs:1249; section
3 of verify-agent-config-distribution.sh) stay valid and green. This phase does
NOT touch them.

**Read the roadmap's Scope section before editing anything** — the sites in this
phase span three different propagation mechanisms, and most live in hand-written
driver regions with no lib and no generator.

**Step 8 added (engine-name single-sourcing).** This phase now also collapses the
hardcoded workflow-engine *name* literals to one canonical list per lane. It is
placed here, and not in its own phase, because this phase already edits every
site that carries those literals — `agent_config.rs`'s `relative_path` values and
`include_str!` paths, `verify-agent-config-distribution.sh`'s pinned `WORKFLOWS`
list, and the generator consumer lists. Phase 7 renames all seven engines to
`rdm-wf-*`; without step 8 that rename must correctly edit ~30 scattered literal
sites in lockstep, which is what made the superseded
`workflow-lane-hardening/phase-1-prefix-workflow-engines-to-distinguish-from-skills`
unplannable (three failed dispatches; the plan author died twice at 83 events
mid-sweep). With step 8, phase 7 edits one list plus the file moves.

   and an `rdmBin` resolver defaulting to `rdm`. Place them per the mechanism that
   owns each region — respecting the no-import constraint, which means the helper
   may need to exist in more than one region rather than being shared.
   `projectFlag(cfg)` is applied ONLY at the call sites that build
   project-scoped commands. The project-agnostic allow-list — sites that must
   carry NO project flag — is `rdm model resolve` and `rdm commit` (plus
   `status`/`discard` if ever added). Every other subcommand used in these
   scripts (`phase list/show/update`, `task list/show/create/update`,
   `worktree add`, `next`, `search`) is project-scoped and takes the flag.

   workflows — this is NOT an open choice. `lib/estimate.mjs` and `estimate.js`

8. **Single-source the workflow-engine name list.** Replace the hardcoded engine
   *name* literals with one canonical list per lane, so phase 7's rename edits a
   list rather than ~30 scattered sites. This is a pure refactor: no name changes,

   verifiable on its own. Sites:

finding.what_fails: For a phase whose branch diff exceeds ~40000 characters (very plausible: the shared-worktree three-dot diff base is cumulative across a roadmap's phases, and this repo's own commits regularly exceed that — e.g. commit 2a025ae alone is 3423 insertions across 28 files), the diff-signals agent truncates diffText per its prompt instructions. Truncated diffText is a non-null, non-empty string, so it never re-triggers deriveSignals'/selectDimensions' documented 'diffText === null -> fail open' escape hatch — it only fires when changedFiles is entirely empty. Two of the three content-derived triggers then have no fallback: `hasUnsafe` (review.mjs:540) is diffText-only with zero path-based signal anywhere, and `publicApiChanged` (review.mjs:534-535) requires the rdm-core/src path match AND a `+pub` diffText match (AND, not OR) — a path hit alone is not sufficient. So a phase that adds a new `unsafe` block or a new public API item past the 40000-char cutoff of a large diff will silently fail to trigger the 'security' or 'api-docs' review dimensions, even though CLAUDE.md requires SAFETY comments and doc-comment sections precisely for those changes.
finding.why: Before this phase, dispatch-phase's code gate never fed deriveSignals a live diff at all — `runCodeReview({ target, ...reviewModels })` was called with no `signals`, which is selectDimensions' fail-open case that always runs every code dimension. This phase is what wires a real (agent-truncated) diffText into the gate for the first time, so it is the change that turns pre-existing gaps in deriveSignals' content-only heuristics (no unsafe path list, AND-not-OR for publicApiChanged) into an exploitable coverage regression versus prior behavior. The code comment at dispatch-phase.js:1259-1261 claims truncation 'only weakens trigger detection toward FAIL-OPEN (a missed trigger costs a dimension that would have run anyway when the file paths already imply it)' — that reasoning holds for `securitySurface` (which has a real path-pattern fallback, SECURITY_PATH_PATTERNS) but is false for `hasUnsafe` (no path fallback exists at all) and only partially true for `publicApiChanged` (path match alone does not satisfy the AND condition).
finding.recommendation: Either (a) give deriveSignals a path-based fallback for hasUnsafe/publicApiChanged so a truncated diffText degrades to 'unknown -> trigger' rather than 'no match -> don't trigger' for these two signals, or (b) have the mechanical diff agent signal truncation explicitly (e.g. a `truncated: true` field) and treat a truncated diffText the same as `diffText === null` in deriveSignals, or (c) raise/eliminate the 40000-char cap for the size of diffs this pipeline actually produces. At minimum, correct the misleading claim in the comment that truncation is always the safe/fail-open direction.

finding.what_fails: None of the three distributed workflow templates threads `agentType` at its mechanical call sites, even though the local .claude/workflows copies do and the trim is measured at 8907 tokens per agent. Every downstream repo that receives the lane therefore pays full price on every mechanical dispatch.
finding.why: A measured, replicated saving is applied locally and withheld from the shipped surface, so the distributed lane is strictly more expensive than the dogfood one for no stated reason.
finding.recommendation: Thread agentType into the distributed templates as well.

provenance.rationale: Divergence-class top-up whose governing artifact is a repo rule with a named owning task.

Not a defect: CLAUDE.md states a downstream repo receives no .claude/agents/ definitions at all and an unresolvable agentType RAISES rather than degrading, so a shipped reference would hard-break every downstream lane on first dispatch. scripts/verify-workflow-review.sh §2b(ii) gates the prohibition, and lifting it is owned by the task ship-mechanical-agent-type-downstream.

finding.concern: architectural-fit
finding.location: .claude/workflows/lib/plan-review.mjs (both runPlanReview call sites)
finding.what_fails: lib/plan-review.mjs calls runPlanReview({ target }) with no `signals` key at either call site, so selectDimensions sees no signals and the `unit-of-work` dimension — whose trigger is targetType === "phase" — is selected for every plan review including task-mode and roadmap-mode ones. The standalone consumer therefore over-selects dimensions relative to the dispatch-phase consumer, which does thread signals.
finding.why: Two consumers of the same pipeline disagree about which dimensions apply to the same target type.
finding.recommendation: Thread targetType-derived signals into both runPlanReview call sites.

provenance.rationale: Divergence-class top-up in PLAN mode, where the corpus is thinner than in code mode.

finding.concern: tests
finding.location: scripts/measure-refuter-severity.mjs (NON_GATING_SEVERITIES) vs .claude/workflows/lib/review.mjs (NON_GATING_SEVERITIES)
finding.what_fails: scripts/measure-refuter-severity.mjs re-declares its own NON_GATING_SEVERITIES constant instead of importing the one in .claude/workflows/lib/review.mjs. If the lane later widens the non-gating set, the measurement instrument keeps reporting against the old set and the projected drop silently becomes wrong.
finding.why: Two copies of the same policy constant in two files is a drift hazard.
finding.recommendation: Import NON_GATING_SEVERITIES from the review lib instead of re-declaring it.

provenance.rationale: Divergence-class top-up whose refutation requires reading the in-file comment that names the gate, not just the two declarations.

groundTruth.evidence: Mechanically true — the constant is declared in both files. Not a defect: the two live in different runtimes and cannot import each other, which the declaration's own comment in scripts/measure-refuter-severity.mjs states, and scripts/verify-token-report.sh greps .claude/workflows/lib/review.mjs for the authoritative value rather than trusting the copy, so drift is gated rather than latent.

finding.concern: correctness
finding.location: rdm-core/src/ops/tag_policy.rs, fn normalize_tag
finding.what_fails: normalize_tag in rdm-core/src/ops/tag_policy.rs lowercases every incoming tag before storing it, which silently contradicts the documented rule that tag matching is exact and case-sensitive. A user who creates the tag `Auth` and then filters on `Auth` gets no results, because the stored value is `auth`.
finding.why: Storage-time normalization and match-time case sensitivity cannot both be correct; one of them is a data-loss bug.
finding.recommendation: Remove the lowercasing from normalize_tag, or document that tags are case-insensitive.

provenance.rationale: False-premise top-up: cites a file and a symbol that do not exist. Refutable by a single existence check, so it separates a refuter that reads from one that reasons from plausibility.

groundTruth.evidence: rdm-core/src/ops/tag_policy.rs does not exist and no `normalize_tag` symbol exists anywhere in the tree. The whole finding rests on a file that is not there.

finding.concern: tests
finding.location: scripts/verify-workflow-review.sh; .claude/workflows/plan-review.js (plan-review-driver block)
finding.what_fails: The plan-review-driver block in .claude/workflows/plan-review.js is a hand-maintained verbatim copy of .claude/workflows/lib/plan-review.mjs, but no harness compares the two. A hand edit to one copy therefore ships a workflow that silently disagrees with the lib every harness actually tests.
finding.why: An ungated verbatim copy of load-bearing logic is drift waiting to happen.
finding.recommendation: Add a byte-identity diff of the plan-review-driver block between the lib and the workflow.

provenance.rationale: False-premise top-up asserting the ABSENCE of a gate that exists — the failure mode of a refuter that greps for the wrong string and concludes nothing is there.

groundTruth.evidence: The gate exists: scripts/verify-workflow-review.sh §5b-drift extracts the plan-review-driver block from both .claude/workflows/lib/plan-review.mjs and .claude/workflows/plan-review.js and fails on any diff, and additionally asserts each copy carries the driver's load-bearing symbols.

finding.concern: correctness
finding.location: scripts/lib/token-report.mjs, fn aggregate
finding.what_fails: aggregate() sums every transcript line it is handed rather than deduping by requestId, so an agent whose usage was streamed across several lines for one request has its output tokens counted several times. Every grouping built on aggregate() (by agent class, by label, by model, by workflow) therefore overstates output.
finding.why: The module header itself states last-write-wins dedupe by requestId is required; the aggregation step does not do it.
finding.recommendation: Dedupe by requestId inside aggregate() before summing.

provenance.rationale: Misread-scope top-up: the stated hazard is real and documented, but it is handled at a different function than the one cited.

groundTruth.evidence: The requestId dedupe is real and required, but it happens in parseAgentTranscript in scripts/lib/token-report.mjs, which builds a per-request Map with last-write-wins semantics. By the time buildRecords hands records to aggregate(), each record already carries deduped per-class totals, so aggregate() has nothing to dedupe. The cited function does not do what the finding says.

finding.concern: correctness
finding.location: .claude/workflows/lib/review.mjs, fn survives (CONFIDENCE_FLOOR)
finding.what_fails: A FAIL criterion emitted by the `ac` dimension is dropped whenever its confidence falls below CONFIDENCE_FLOOR, because survives() applies the floor to everything the finders return. A genuinely failing acceptance criterion reported at 65 confidence therefore never reaches classifyOutcome and the phase is reported reviewed.
finding.why: The acceptance-criteria gate is the one check that must not be defeasible by a confidence heuristic.
finding.recommendation: Exempt ac-dimension results from the confidence floor.

provenance.rationale: Misread-scope top-up: the floor is real and does apply to findings, but the AC table travels on a separate channel that never passes through it.

groundTruth.evidence: survives() and CONFIDENCE_FLOOR are real, but the AC table is returned as STRUCTURED DATA separate from the findings list and is checked directly by acTableHasGap — the spec prose in .claude/workflows/lib/review.mjs states that a surviving FAIL/PARTIAL criterion "is checked directly against that table, never through finding severity or the refute/confidence-floor path, so the guarantee cannot be silently defeated by a refuter or the 70-point floor". The property is true of findings, not of the channel the finding cites.

finding.concern: architecture
finding.location: scripts/lib/token-report.mjs (mixed use of ?? and || for defaulting)
finding.what_fails: The module defaults some values with `??` and others with `||`, so a reader cannot tell at a glance whether a falsy-but-valid 0 is intended to survive. Standardizing on `??` would make the intent uniform.
finding.why: Mixed defaulting operators in one module are a readability and review-cost problem.
finding.recommendation: Standardize on ?? throughout.

provenance.rationale: Style-preference top-up: a true observation with no defect behind it, to check whether a tier confuses taste with correctness.

groundTruth.evidence: Both operators appear in scripts/lib/token-report.mjs and each use is correct for its site; preferring one uniformly is a taste call a reasonable reviewer could go either way on.

finding.concern: architecture
finding.location: scripts/verify-*.sh (each defines its own say/pass/fail helpers)
finding.what_fails: Every verify-*.sh harness defines its own say/pass/fail helpers rather than sourcing a shared one, so the same handful of functions is written out a dozen times and their output formats can drift apart.
finding.why: Duplicated helper definitions across a dozen scripts are a maintenance cost.
finding.recommendation: Extract them into scripts/lib/ and source it.

provenance.rationale: Style-preference top-up in the shell surface, where the repo already has a shared-lib precedent (scripts/lib/mechanical-tier-check.sh) so the argument is genuinely two-sided.

groundTruth.evidence: The duplication is real, and scripts/lib/mechanical-tier-check.sh shows the repo will share shell helpers when it wants to — but keeping each harness self-contained is a defensible choice for hermetic gates. No behavior is wrong either way.
